greeting: Good morning, Bay View, and happy Monday. It's a frosty 30 degrees out there, but the sun takes over today with a high near 51, and the week keeps warming toward 60 by Thursday. Leaf pickup got a reprieve through Nov. 29, Rush-Mor Records is in the spotlight, and our history corner climbs St. Augustine's steeple.

top.title: Teen wounded in early Sunday shooting near Burrell and Smith streets
top.dek: An 18-year-old was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries; police are still looking for a suspect.
top.body:
Milwaukee police are investigating a shooting that happened just after 2 a.m. Sunday, Nov. 15, near S. Burrell Street and E. Smith Street in Bay View. An 18-year-old was taken to a hospital with gunshot wounds that police describe as not life-threatening.

No arrest had been announced as of Sunday night, and police have not said what led up to the gunfire. A neighbor's doorbell camera picked up the sound of the shots, according to WISN 12.

The shooting was one of several non-fatal shootings across the city over the weekend. Anyone with information can call MPD at 414-935-7360, or reach Crime Stoppers anonymously at 414-224-TIPS or through the P3 Tips app.

image.alt: Milwaukee police squad cars parked on a residential street at night

top.title: Milwaukee's leaf pickup now runs through Nov. 29
top.dek: DPW pushed back Sunday's deadline so late-dropping trees can still be raked to the street or bagged.
top.body:
The city's Department of Public Works has extended fall leaf collection through Sunday, Nov. 29. The original deadline was this past Sunday, but many trees, including plenty in Bay View, are still dropping leaves.

Rake leaves into the street with roughly a foot of space between the pile and the curb so water can still reach the drains, or set them at the curb in paper yard bags. A live map on the city's website shows where crews are working.

Neighbors told FOX6 they remember last year, when an early snow buried leaf piles and contributed to street flooding, so it's worth getting leaves out sooner rather than later.

image.alt: A large pile of raked leaves and a paper yard-waste bag at the edge of a residential street

openings.title: Torzala and Component plan Black Friday beers at the Lincoln Warehouse
openings.dek: Both breweries in the Lincoln Warehouse have special releases lined up for Nov. 27.
openings.body:
Two breweries in the Lincoln Warehouse on Bay View's western edge are on OnMilwaukee's list of Black Friday beer releases. Brewing Torzala will pour two specials in its second-floor taproom: the third batch of its Cream City Calling cream ale, made with honey, Door County cherries and cranberries, and a new altbier named for local musician Juan Avalos.

Both Torzala beers will be on tap and sold in limited four-packs. Component Brewing, in the same building, plans to release its barrel-aged Swirl stout along with a new barrel-aged barleywine.

Black Friday is Nov. 27. Check each brewery's social media for hours and can limits.

image.alt: Two glasses of beer on the bar in front of the tap list at Brewing Torzala

schools.title: MPS Great Schools committee holds its last scheduled meeting tonight
schools.dek: The panel is drafting school-closure criteria and building recommendations. It meets 6-8 p.m. at North Division.
schools.body:
The Milwaukee Public Schools Great Schools Advisory Committee meets tonight, Monday, Nov. 16, from 6 to 8 p.m. at North Division High School, 1011 W. Center St. It is the last meeting on the committee's current schedule, and the public can attend.

MPS formed the committee to come up with criteria for closing schools, recommend specific schools to close and suggest where the district should build. Final decisions stay with the superintendent and the school board.

Those recommendations could reach any MPS building, including the ones Bay View families use, so tonight is a chance to see where the work stands. Visitors can also tour recent improvements at North Division.

image.alt: Audience members watching a presentation at an MPS Great Schools Advisory Committee meeting
image.credit: Jonathan Aguilar / Milwaukee Neighborhood News Service / CatchLight Local

help.title: City-county Holiday Drive opens today, collecting food and essentials
help.dek: Drop off food, tote bags, wipes or toiletries at libraries, City Hall and more for a Metcalfe Park pantry.
help.body:
Mayor Cavalier Johnson and County Board Chair Marcelia Nicholson-Bovell are launching the 2026 Holiday Drive Monday morning. The city and county have run the drive every year since 2007.

Organizers are asking for food, reusable tote bags, baby wipes, deodorant and other everyday essentials. This year's donations go to the Metcalfe Park People's Pantry, which Metcalfe Park Community Bridges runs.

There are nine drop-off sites. The closest to Bay View are the Zablocki Branch Library, 3501 W. Oklahoma Ave., and the City Hall rotunda, 200 E. Wells St. Other sites include East Branch Library, the County Courthouse and the Milwaukee County Zoo.

image.alt: A volunteer stocking a community fridge with apples and eggs
image.credit: Jonathan Aguilar / Milwaukee Neighborhood News Service / CatchLight Local

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Rush-Mor Records
spotlight.dek: Milwaukee's oldest record store has been spinning on the corner of KK and Potter since 1971
spotlight.body:
Long before Kinnickinnic Avenue filled up with cocktail bars and boutiques, there was a record store on the corner of KK and Potter. Rush-Mor Records, at 2635 S. Kinnickinnic Ave., opened in 1971 and bills itself as Milwaukee's oldest record store, a title local press has repeated for years. It still sells new and used vinyl, CDs, DVDs, band T-shirts and imports from around the world.

The shop has been run since 1994 by Dan DuChaine and Bill Rouleau. As Milwaukee Record has told it, Rouleau was working part-time at the store when he heard the original owner was thinking about closing. He called DuChaine that fall, and the two agreed to give it a year. That trial run is now past the 30-year mark. DuChaine told Milwaukee Magazine in 2017 that the store had outlasted CD burning, downloads, file sharing and recessions, crediting loyal customers for keeping it going.

The racks lean toward modern rock, punk and hardcore, progressive and Euro-rock, rockabilly and heavy metal, and the shop will special-order what it doesn't have. Local releases get real shelf space, including a dedicated section for the Milwaukee label Triple Eye Industries. Radio Milwaukee's 2023 Record Store Day profile described a tin ceiling, string lights and a corner of band shirts, plus owners who want first-timers to feel at ease. The staff has some longevity too: CBS 58 reported that Billy Swinger has worked there for about 30 years. The shop dog, Wolfgang, also greets visitors.

Rush-Mor's reach extends beyond its four walls. It curates a music stage at the Bay View Bash street festival each September, which Milwaukee Record has called the Bash's longest-running stage, and it backs 91.7 WMSE and the MKEpunk archive of Milwaukee punk recordings. During the 2020 Safer at Home order, the store offered curbside pickup and delivery and hid 64 oversized crayons around Bay View for a free neighborhood scavenger hunt, Urban Milwaukee reported.

What's new: earlier this month the shop wrapped up a giveaway of a band-signed test pressing of My Chemical Romance's The Black Parade, marking the album's 20th anniversary. Rush-Mor also launched a refreshed website this year, and its full inventory of new arrivals, used stock and collectibles is listed on Discogs for anyone who can't make it in. Instagram is where it announces new arrivals and in-store happenings.

Rush-Mor Records, 2635 S. Kinnickinnic Ave., (414) 481-6040. Open noon to 6 pm Tuesday through Sunday; closed Mondays. rushmor.com, Instagram @rushmorrecords.

buzz.headline: Ticket blitz: every car on one Logan Ave. block got a citation
buzz.body: A neighbor posted Saturday morning that their son walked out to find a parking ticket on every single car on their stretch of Logan Avenue, with no clue why. The post drew more than 120 comments, with neighbors trading theories and asking whether some sign or rule had changed overnight. The city hasn't said what prompted it; if you got one, the ticket itself lists the violation and how to contest it.

buzz.body: Reservations-only no more, at least at the bar: starting Wednesday, Nov. 18, Barnacle Bud's winter supper club is holding its six bar seats for walk-ins every Wednesday through Dec. 30, first come, first served. Bar-only specials include a $30 steak frites and $9 brandy old fashioneds. Diners who bring food donations for the Bay View Community Center also get a free ice cream drink.

buzz.headline: Leave the leaves? The yard debate rages on as pickup gets extended
buzz.body: A shared post urging people to leave fallen leaves on their yards for pollinators and wildlife racked up nearly 200 reactions and dozens of comments in Bay View Town Hall. Fans called it free mulch; skeptics shared stories of critters and soggy lawns. Either way, the city's rake-out deadline is now Nov. 29.

image.credit: Mikael Kristenson, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

history.title: St. Augustine's steeple rises over Howell Avenue
history.text: In November 1908, Bay View's German Catholics dedicated St. Augustine of Hippo Church on Howell Avenue, the Brust & Philipp landmark still standing 118 years later.
history.body:
In November 1908, Bay View's German-speaking Catholics moved into the building that still anchors Howell Avenue. St. Augustine of Hippo Church was dedicated on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26, 1908, by Milwaukee Archbishop Sebastian Messmer, a little more than seven months after its cornerstone was laid on Palm Sunday.

The parish was barely two decades old. Around 47 families organized it in 1887 so they could hear sermons in German without traveling across town, and they bought lots at Howell Avenue and Graham Street. (The parish's own history lists 1887 as its founding, while its first pastor, the Rev. Peter Schumacher, was appointed and first Mass said in 1888.) For nearly 20 years the congregation worshipped upstairs in a combined church and school at Homer and Graham streets, with classrooms below.

In December 1906 parishioners voted to build a proper church for no more than $36,000. They hired Brust & Philipp, a prominent Milwaukee firm, whose Romanesque revival design in cream brick gave the neighborhood the tall steeple, rose window and triple arched entrances still visible today. Three days after the dedication, the Blessed Sacrament was carried in procession from the old church to the new one.

The building kept filling in over the years: a pipe organ in 1910, three steeple bells in 1914, side and main altars in the 1920s and '30s. During World War I the parish quietly dropped German from its bulletins and sermons. By 1973 it counted roughly 1,300 families, and the four-faced steeple clock added in 2006 has become a Howell Avenue landmark of its own.

St. Augustine is still an active parish at 2530 S. Howell Ave., and it opens its doors each fall for Doors Open Milwaukee and its Oktoberfest, a nod to those German founders.
